Federal Reserve Board announces enforcement action with Coastal Trust Company

Published 2026-10-05 22:30 UTC

The Federal Reserve Board on Friday announced an enforcement action with Coastal Trust Company, Charleston, South Carolina, a state member bank, to address deficiencies in the bank's anti-money-laundering and sanctions compliance programs.

Examiners found that the bank failed to maintain an effective program for monitoring transactions and filing suspicious activity reports, particularly for accounts opened through its correspondent banking business. The bank's customer due diligence procedures did not adequately identify high-risk customers, and its transaction monitoring system had not been updated to reflect changes in the bank's business.

Under the written agreement, the bank must submit within 90 days an enhanced compliance program that includes updated risk assessments, improved customer due diligence, and stronger oversight by the board of directors. The bank must also engage an independent consultant to review account and transaction activity over the past two years and report any suspicious activity that was not previously identified.

The agreement requires the bank to strengthen its management of compliance staffing and training, and to provide quarterly progress reports to the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond. The bank's board must approve the plans before they are submitted.

The Board said the action does not require the bank to pay a civil money penalty at this time, but that it may take further action if the deficiencies are not corrected. Coastal Trust Company has consented to the agreement without admitting or denying the findings.

The written agreement is attached. The Board publishes enforcement actions so that the public is informed about the supervisory issues identified at banks it oversees. Inquiries about the action should be directed to the Board's public affairs office.

The agreement also requires the bank to review its correspondent accounts with foreign financial institutions and to close accounts where it cannot obtain adequate information about the underlying customers. Progress on these steps will be reviewed during the next scheduled examination of the bank.
